Honest, muted color: No color grading tricks. The color is what was there, rendered faithfully and quietly.
Complex layered compositions: 3+ distinct planes of action in a single frame — each could be its own photograph
Red filter skies: Dramatically darkened blue skies that separate clouds and mountain peaks. Blue channel pulled to near-black in the gray conversion.
Film still aesthetic (Untitled Film Stills, 1977–1980): Black-and-white, but her color work carries the same DNA — as if they're production stills from movies that don't exist
Hyper-real saturation: Colors pushed beyond natural into a pop art dimension. Red is RED. Blue is BLUE.
Extreme geometric contrast: Backlit silhouettes against bright geometric light shafts
Cinematic teal/cool shadows: The defining color move. Shadows go blue/teal.
Moderate contrast: Not Ansel Adams dramatic, not flat. Natural tonal transitions.
Cape Cod golden light: The defining characteristic of his later masterwork. Warm, hazy, almost tangible — light you can feel.
Ring flash pop: Shadowless, flat lighting that saturates colors and eliminates depth. Like a specimen under a microscope.
Long exposure smoothness: Water becomes mist, clouds become streaks, people vanish
Direct flash aesthetic: Hard shadows behind subjects, red-eye, blown highlights on faces — the snapshot turned art
Lifted midtones: Blacks are never truly black. Shadows breathe. The entire image floats in Zone IV–VII.
Through-glass softness: Reflections on top of subjects, double exposures from window glass
Biblical luminance: Highlights that seem to glow from within. Zones VIII–IX placed deliberately.
Afghan Girl palette: Warm skin tones against cool/neutral backgrounds. The red-green contrast.
Pastel palette: Lavender, mint, blush pink, butter yellow, powder blue — never saturated, always soft
Cool blue/magenta night cast: The streetlight spectrum — sodium vapor (warm) mixed with fluorescent/LED (cool) creates distinctive magenta-blue shadows
Square format aesthetic: Central compositions, balanced geometries
Ordinary subjects, extraordinary color: A red ceiling, a blue tricycle, a green freezer — the color IS the subject
